evidence: Suet. Gram. 7.2: nec unquam dē mercēdibus pactus, he never bargained over his fees
Plaut. Bacch. 865–866: pacīscī cum illō paululā pecūniā potes, you can strike a bargain with him for a little money
terms.comment: pacīscor is to bargain, to settle terms (with long ī, de Vaan 452, pacīscere); once buyer and seller agree, dē pretiō convēnit (Quint. 4.2.41).

evidence: Liv. 22.56.3: in captīvōrum pretiīs … nec magnī ducis mōre nūndinantem, haggling over the prisoners’ ransoms, not as a great general would
terms.comment: Properly to trade at the market (nūndinae, with long ū, de Vaan 415); said with contempt of haggling, and of trafficking in what should not be sold (Cic. Phil. 3.10, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Plaut. Merc. 441: nē licitēre advorsum meī animī sententiam, don’t go bidding against my wishes
Comen. OP 126: Ēmptor licitātur, et pretium offert
terms.comment: In Plautus to bid against a rival buyer; Comenius uses it of the customer making his offer at a stall.

phrases.latin: In portum vēnī, nāvem prōspexī, quantī veheret interrogāvī, dē pretiō convēnit, cōnscendī, sublātae sunt ancorae, solvimus ōram, profectī sumus.
phrases.english: I came to the harbour, looked over a ship, asked what the fare was, we agreed on the price, I went aboard, the anchors were weighed, we cast off and set out.

phrases.latin: praetereā cōmī facilīque nātūrā, nec unquam dē mercēdibus pactus, eōque plūra ex līberālitāte discentium cōnsecūtus
phrases.english: a kindly, easy-going man besides, who never bargained over his fees and so received all the more from his pupils’ generosity

phrases.latin: Vēnditor ostentat rem prōmercālem, et indicat pretium, quantī liceat. Ēmptor licitātur, et pretium offert.
phrases.english: The seller shows his goods and names the price, what they cost; the buyer bargains and offers a price.

sources: Lewis & Short: paciscor · Lewis & Short: nundinor · Lewis & Short: licitor
